result: IL-1 signaling is required for normal wound closure kinetics and interfollicular epidermal (IFE) stem cell proliferation during wound healing. IL1R KO mice display a 2-day delay in wound closure that manifests significantly at day 3 post-wounding, and IFE stem cell proliferation is significantly impaired in the absence of IL-1 signaling. Epidermal hyperplasia proximal to wounds is also diminished without IL-1 signaling.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C13 are supported by wound closure kinetics data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), quantitative IFE proliferation measurements (Figure 1A), and epidermal thickness measurements (Figure 1D). The data show statistically significant differences between WT and IL1R KO mice at appropriate time points, with proper controls and replication.

result: Hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs) exhibit IL-1-dependent proliferation in response to wounding. CD34+ HFSCs are highly proliferative in follicles proximal to wounds but quiescent distally. HFSC proliferation is significantly reduced in IL1R KO mice starting at day 1 post-wounding and persisting throughout the proliferative phase. This is corroborated by Sox9+ HFSC staining showing substantial increases in wounded skin that are reduced without IL-1 signaling.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 and C21-C22 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 1B, 1C, 1—figure supplement 3, 1—figure supplement 4, 1—figure supplement 6) showing Ki67+/CD34+ and Sox9+ HFSCs at multiple time points with quantification. The spatial and temporal patterns are clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: The Casp8 cKO mouse model recapitulates wound-like phenotypes including epidermal thickening and increased stem cell proliferation. The model shows a thicker epidermis than WT, which is significantly reduced (but not to WT levels) by removing IL-1 signaling. The Casp8 cKO skin exhibits more than two-fold increased HFSC proliferation compared to WT, which decreases by ~30% without IL-1 signaling.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C18-C20, and C23 are supported by histological data (Figure 1E), immunofluorescence (Figure 1F), and quantification (Figures 1G, 1H) showing epidermal thickness and stem cell proliferation across genotypes. The partial rescue by IL-1R deletion (C23) is appropriately acknowledged and discussed in the context of system redundancy (C24).

result: IL-1α is neither necessary nor sufficient to induce HFSC migration. While HFSCs show >3-fold increased chemotaxis in response to Casp8 cKO conditioned media, IL1R KO HFSCs remain responsive to this chemotactic cue, and recombinant IL-1 alone cannot induce HFSC migration.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by transwell migration assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 7) showing that IL-1R-deficient HFSCs can still migrate in response to wound CM and that rhIL-1 alone is insufficient. This clearly separates IL-1's role in proliferation from migration, though the identity of the actual chemotactic factor remains unknown.

result: Macrophages and granulocytes are increased in Casp8 cKO skin, and their numbers are markedly reduced in the absence of either IL-1 signaling or γδT-cells. The impairment of immune cell recruitment in γδT-cell-deficient mice is similar to that observed upon removal of IL-1 signaling.
evaluation: Claims C32, C33, C37, and C38 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2A) showing Mac1+ and Gr-1+ cells across different genotypes. The similar phenotypes in IL1R KO and γδT-cell KO mice suggest an epistatic relationship, though the mechanistic connection requires further investigation.

result: γδT-cell numbers are increased in Casp8 cKO mice but dramatically reduced without IL-1 signaling. Loss of γδT-cells significantly reduces epidermal thickness and HFSC proliferation in both the Casp8 cKO model and excisional wounds, with a more pronounced impact on HFSCs than IFE cells.
evaluation: Claims C39-C46 are supported by immunofluorescence and EdU labeling data (Figures 2B-E, 2—figure supplements 1-4) showing γδT-cell numbers, HFSC proliferation, and epidermal thickness across genotypes. The differential effect on HFSCs versus IFE cells (C44) is clearly demonstrated with quantification (Figure 2E).

result: IL-1α levels are comparable in Casp8 cKO skin with or without γδT-cells, and in wounded WT versus γδT-cell KO skin. Despite normal IL-1α levels, active γδT-cells are necessary for early HFSC proliferation, suggesting IL-1 signaling converges upon γδT-cells to mediate epithelial stem cell proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplements 5, 7) and ELISA data (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) showing no significant differences in IL-1α levels between genotypes. The inference that IL-1 acts through γδT-cells (C50) is reasonable given the epistatic relationship demonstrated, though direct mechanistic proof would require additional experiments.

result: γδT-cell proliferation is increased three-fold in Casp8 cKO skin and significantly decreased without IL-1 signaling, both in the genetic model and in excisional wounds. γδT-cell activation (measured by TNFα expression) is also increased in Casp8 cKO and markedly reduced without IL-1 signaling, though some residual proliferation remains in the double knockout.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are supported by quantitative data (Figure 3A) and immunofluorescence (Figures 3B-C, 3—figure supplements 1-2) showing γδT-cell proliferation and activation markers. The acknowledgment of residual proliferation in the dKO (C59) appropriately recognizes system redundancy.

result: IL-7 expression is upregulated in Casp8 cKO skin and is not affected by the absence of IL-1 signaling or γδT-cells. This establishes that IL-7 is independently regulated from IL-1 and γδT-cells.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5) showing IL-7 expression levels across genotypes with no significant differences between Casp8 cKO and double knockouts. This is important for establishing IL-7 as a constitutive signal that synergizes with IL-1.

result: IL-1α and IL-7 work synergistically to expand activated γδT-cell populations. In vitro proliferation assays show that γδT-cells treated with Casp8 cKO CM exhibit 2.5-fold increased proliferation, which is significantly reduced by blocking either IL-1 or IL-7 signaling. The effect is enhanced when both pathways are blocked together. Simply adding recombinant IL-1 and IL-7 to normal media is sufficient to reconstitute the proliferation observed with Casp8 cKO CM.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C68-C75 are strongly supported by in vitro γδT-cell proliferation data (Figure 3D) showing dose-response relationships, blocking experiments, and reconstitution with recombinant cytokines. The synergistic interaction is clearly demonstrated through additive effects of blocking both pathways and sufficiency of both cytokines together.

result: IL-1α-dependent stimulation of dermal fibroblasts preferentially stimulates IFE cell proliferation. Conditioned media from activated fibroblasts causes dramatic increases in IFE proliferation and modest increases in HFSC proliferation, both of which are reduced to control levels without IL-1 signaling. This suggests IFE cells preferentially respond to mesenchymal signals.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C76-C80 are supported by in vitro proliferation assays (Figures 4A-B, 4—figure supplement 1) showing differential effects of activated fibroblast CM on IFE versus HFSC proliferation. The IL-1 dependence is clearly demonstrated by loss of effect in IL1R KO fibroblasts.

result: Activated γδT-cells preferentially stimulate HFSC proliferation. Treatment with Casp8 cKO CM activates γδT-cells (increased FGF7 and TNFα expression), and CM from activated γδT-cells causes significant HFSC proliferation. While activated γδT-cells can also stimulate IFE proliferation, the effect on HFSCs is 40% greater. Recombinant IL-1α or IL-7 alone is sufficient to induce maximal FGF7 expression and recapitulate HFSC proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C2 and C83-C88, C96 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 4C) showing γδT-cell activation markers and in vitro proliferation assays (Figure 4D) demonstrating preferential effects on HFSCs. The differential response is quantified and statistically significant.

result: Combined treatment with conditioned media from both activated dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells substantially increases proliferation rates of both IFE cells and HFSCs, suggesting additive or synergistic effects.
evaluation: Claim C89 is supported by in vitro proliferation data (Figure 4E) showing that combining CM from both cell types increases proliferation beyond either alone. This demonstrates that both pathways can contribute to stem cell proliferation.

result: Both activated dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells secrete FGF7, but only γδT-cells secrete IL1F8/IL-36β, which was recently shown to promote stem cell proliferation. This differential cytokine secretion may explain the preferential effects on different stem cell populations.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3) showing differential expression of these factors and citation to Yang et al., 2010 for IL1F8/IL-36β function. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the differential effects observed.

result: The downregulation of epidermal caspase-8 is a normal wound healing phenomenon that leads to IL-1α release, which mediates dermal fibroblast activation and epidermal stem cell stimulation. The conditional ablation of caspase-8 recapitulates wound healing features. IL-1 signaling partners with constitutively secreted IL-7 to expand active γδT-cell populations, which then stimulate HFSC proliferation and mobilization for wound repair.
evaluation: Claims C97-C103 synthesize the major findings and are supported by the collective data from the manuscript and citations to prior work (Lee et al., 2009). The model integrates the IL-1/IL-7/γδT-cell/HFSC axis demonstrated throughout the study, though the mobilization aspect (C103) is more inferential.

result: Blocking IL-1R1 signaling does not completely impair wound repair, likely due to compensatory mechanisms involving other IL-1 family members (IL-1F6, IL-1F8) that signal through the IL-36 receptor. In complex systems like wound healing, removal of individual components impedes kinetics rather than completely inhibiting the process.
evaluation: Claims C108, C109, C114, and C115 are supported by wound closure data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing delayed but not absent healing in IL1R KO mice, and by the observation that IL-1R deletion doesn't fully rescue the Casp8 cKO phenotype (Figure 1E). The explanation invoking IL-1 family redundancy is reasonable given the known biology, though direct testing would require additional experiments.

result: IL-1 and IL-7 have been shown to work synergistically to increase γδT-cell proliferation in the newborn thymus, consistent with the observations in skin wound healing.
evaluation: Claims C62 and C120 are supported by citation to Lynch and Shevach, 1992, providing precedent for the IL-1/IL-7 synergy observed in the current study. This strengthens the mechanistic interpretation of the skin wound healing data.

result: The findings are consistent with prior work showing that optimal γδT-cell activation is required for HFSC proliferation and efficient wound closure. The age-related decline in wound healing correlates with documented changes in IL-1 family cytokines during aging.
evaluation: Claims C123 and C124 are supported by citations to Keyes et al., 2016 and Ye et al., 2002, placing the current findings in the context of prior literature and suggesting broader implications for age-related wound healing defects.

result: Background on γδT-cell biology: Following wounding, γδT-cells become activated and promote epidermal stem cell proliferation by secreting KGF/FGF7. Wound healing is impaired in γδT-cell-deficient mice. γδT-cell activation depends on recognition of stress signals from keratinocytes, including increased CAR expression recognized by JAML on γδT-cells. Keratinocytes constitutively express IL-7, which is required for γδT-cell development.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36, C51-C55, C63-C64 represent established knowledge supported by multiple citations (Jameson and Havran, 2007; Jameson et al., 2002, 2005; Witherden et al., 2010; Witherden and Havran, 2011). These provide necessary background context for interpreting the current findings.

result: Macrophages and granulocytes are among the earliest inflammatory cells responding to injury and are known to enhance epidermal stem cell proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 represent established knowledge supported by citation to Martin, 1997, providing context for the immune cell recruitment data.

result: γδT-cells have been found to stimulate hair neogenesis via Fgf9. There is heterogeneity among cutaneous γδT-cells: dermal γδT-cells secrete Fgf9 while epidermal γδT-cells (DETCs) secrete IL-1F8, which does not promote hair neogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119 are supported by citations to Gay et al., 2013 and Yang et al., 2010, highlighting the complexity of γδT-cell populations and their differential functions. This provides important context for interpreting the HFSC proliferation data.

result: Transgenic mice overexpressing IL-1F6 develop severe cutaneous inflammation. Activated γδT-cells release IL-1F8, which promotes stem cell proliferation. IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 signal through the IL-36 receptor and induce mitogenic factors.
evaluation: Claims C110-C113 are supported by citations to Blumberg et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010; and Towne et al., 2004, providing mechanistic context for IL-1 family redundancy and alternative signaling pathways.

result: IL-1α-mediated induction of keratinocyte proliferation factors from dermal fibroblasts is one mechanism for epidermal stem cell proliferation. IL-1α can also stimulate epidermal keratinocyte migration.
evaluation: Claims C17 and C25 are supported by citations to prior work (Lee et al., 2009; Chen et al., 1995) and by current data (Figure 4A-B), establishing the fibroblast-mediated pathway as a parallel mechanism to the γδT-cell pathway.

result: Other factors, such as leukocyte-derived signals, contribute to stem cell proliferation in wound microenvironments, explaining why IL-1 signaling removal doesn't completely eliminate wound phenotypes.
evaluation: Claim C24 is supported by citation to Eming et al., 2007 and by inference from the incomplete rescue observed in IL1R KO mice. This appropriately acknowledges system complexity and redundancy.

result: The differential proliferation of IFE cells and HFSCs is probably due to differences in cytokine cocktails secreted by fibroblasts versus γδT-cells. IL1F8 signals through the IL-36 receptor, and HFSCs may be more susceptible to its mitogenic effects.
evaluation: Claims C90, C94, and C95 are speculative interpretations of the differential effects observed. While the differential cytokine secretion is documented (C91-C92), the mechanistic explanation for why HFSCs respond preferentially remains hypothetical and would require direct testing of IL-36 receptor expression and signaling in different stem cell populations.

result: In WT mouse backskin, γδT-cells are found in close association with the HFSC niche, while dermal fibroblasts are in close apposition to IFE cells in the basal epidermis. This spatial relationship may explain differential effects on stem cell populations.
evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009. Claim C82 is based on established skin anatomy. Together, these provide a spatial explanation for the differential effects observed, though direct demonstration of this spatial relationship in the current study would strengthen the argument.

result: As wound healing progresses, other infiltrating cells may contribute to stem cell proliferation. Wounded keratinocytes produce CCL2 to attract macrophages, which secrete IL-1β (more potent than IL-1α) to induce hair regrowth. This synergistic interaction between IL-1 and IL-7 is probably a response to seal wounds quickly and increase epithelial stem cell pools.
evaluation: Claims C104-C107, C121-C122 are largely speculative, connecting known biology (C105, C107 supported by citations) with hypothetical mechanisms (C106, C121, C122). While the speculation is reasonable given the known redundancy and the incomplete phenotypes in single knockouts, these claims represent future directions rather than demonstrated findings.

result: The truncated lifespan of Casp8 cKO mice (~20 days) and chronic inflammation prevent investigation of hair regeneration cycles. The location of proliferation-inducing cells may impact which stem cell pool they affect.
evaluation: Claim C125 is an observational statement about the model's limitations. Claim C126 is speculative reasoning about spatial effects. Both are appropriately acknowledged as limitations and hypotheses rather than tested conclusions.

result: There is an emerging paradigm that immune-associated signals regulate stem cell homeostasis. The increased proliferation in Casp8 cKO can be attained through keratinocyte-fibroblast or keratinocyte-γδT-cell interactions, analogous to tumor-stroma interactions. Understanding wound-associated stem cell proliferation may illuminate tumor initiation pathways.
evaluation: Claims C127-C131 place the findings in broader context. C127 is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015. C128 is supported by the current data. C129 and C130 are supported by citations to McAllister and Weinberg, 2010 and Arwert et al., 2010. C131 is speculative but reasonable given the wound-tumor parallels.

result: Methods: Epidermis-specific caspase-8 knockouts were generated by crossing Casp8 fl/fl mice to Krt14-Cre mice. IL1R−/− mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory. All animals were on a C57BL/6 background.
evaluation: Claims C132-C134 describe standard methods supported by appropriate citations (Beisner et al., 2005; Vasioukhin et al., 1999) and vendor information. These are factual statements about experimental design.
